protagonist.name: Maya
protagonist.description: young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat

video_prompts.prompt: Wide shot of a dark, empty space. A single, glowing white line representing the number line stretches across the screen. Maya, a young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat, stands beside it. Luminous points appear at intervals, labeled -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. Maya gestures, and the gaps between integers populate with pulsing blue dots, representing rational numbers. Then, a smooth, continuous stream of green light flows, filling every remaining micro-gap, representing irrational numbers. The camera performs a slow dolly zoom forward along the line, showing it become a solid, unbroken continuum of light. Final frame: a close-up on a segment of the solid, glowing line, showing no gaps at all.

A sterile, white laboratory. Maya, a young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat, stands before a holographic pedestal. A large, complex crystal representing the number 360 hovers above it. Maya uses a holographic tool to touch the crystal. It fractures cleanly into its fundamental prime components: three glowing blue cubes (2s), two red pyramids (3s), and one yellow sphere (5). These basic shapes float in a collection, separate but distinct. The camera orbits the initial crystal, then pushes in to capture the moment of fracture. Final frame: a static shot of the separated, glowing prime-factor shapes, proving that the composite number is built uniquely from these indivisible prime elements.

In a holographic lab, Maya, a young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat, observes two floating collections of prime factors. On the left, for the number 180, are two blue cubes (2s), two red pyramids (3s), and one yellow sphere (5). On the right, for 308, are two blue cubes (2s), one green octahedron (7), and one purple icosahedron (11). Maya gestures, and only the common factors—the two blue cubes from each set—glow intensely. They slide to a central area and merge into a single block labeled 'HCF = 4'. The non-common factors fade to grey. The camera pans from left to right, then zooms into the central merge. Final frame: a close-up on the glowing HCF block.

In an abstract dark space, a large, glowing balance scale is at the center. Maya, a young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat, observes it. On one side sits a shimmering, unstable orb labeled √2. On the other, two stacks of solid blocks, 'p' and 'q', keep the scale perfectly level. A red light scans the 'p' stack, which splits into two even halves. A blue light then scans the 'q' stack, which also splits. A red 'CONTRADICTION' alert flashes as this violates the 'coprime' rule. The scale violently tips, shattering the block stacks. The camera holds steady, then zooms in on the splitting action before pulling back as the scale collapses. Final frame: The √2 orb floats alone, stable and glowing.

In a bright workshop, Maya, a young scientist with short black hair, white lab coat, stands before a large digital canvas. Two numbers, 72 and 120, appear as rectangular areas made of their prime factor blocks. Maya extracts the common blocks (2^3 and 3) to form a small rectangle labeled 'HCF = 24'. She then gathers the highest power of all blocks (2^3, 3^2, and 5) to form a large rectangle labeled 'LCM = 360'. The HCF and LCM rectangles are placed next to a combined rectangle of the original two numbers, 'Product = 8640'. The areas are shown to be equal. The camera does a top-down crane shot, showing the areas being measured and compared. Final frame: A split screen showing 'HCF x LCM' on one side and 'Product' on the other, with a glowing equals sign.
